newsitem.title: USA: Crews reopen track near Arizona derailment site.
newsitem.headline: Crews reopen track near Arizona derailment site.

text.p: Workers Sunday reopened a portion of railroad track where an Amtrak train derailed in the Arizona desert and officials said a buckled bridge at the site of the accident could be open by Monday.

The track was reopened after workers spent hours clearing debris from the four-engine, 16-car Southwest Chief train that jumped the tracks Saturday while enroute to Chicago from Los Angeles. More than 150 people were injured.
"The track is available and freight is moving through there right now," said Debbie Hare, an Amtrak spokeswoman in Chicago. "That's really good news because it's a busy area."

Rail traffic had been at a standstill since early Saturday when the train derailed about 13 miles east of Kingman, a small community about 100 miles southeast of Las Vegas. The tracks, which are owned and operated by Burlington Northern Santa Fe Railways Corp., were shut down immediately.

Investigators from the National Transportation Safety Board were still on the scene Sunday trying to determine the cause of the derailment. Authorities believe a small bridge was weakened and then buckled when a flash flood hit the area early Saturday, causing the normally dry wash underneath to swell with water.
Ironically, the bridge and the track apparently had been checked just hours before the derailment and were declared to be in good condition.
The derailment is the second major train crash in Arizona in nearly two years.

Amtrak's Sunset Limited derailed in October 1995 in a remote area about 55 miles southwest of Phoenix. One person was killed and 78 were injured in that accident, which investigators determined was the result of tampering with a track and a warning system. No one has been arrested for that incident and an investigation continues.
